Title: H5N1-Pandemie bei Menschen "unwahrscheinlich"

Summary: 
The highly pathogenic H5N1 avian influenza virus, which has caused significant ecological and economic damage globally, is currently circulating widely among wild and domestic animals but is considered 'unlikely' to cause an imminent human pandemic, according to virologist Florian Krammer at a conference hosted by the Austrian Agency for Health and Food Safety (AGES). The virus, classified as clade 2.3.4.4b and first identified in 2020, is described by Krammer as a 'very fit' variant. While human infections have been rare in Europe—mostly mild—there are concerns about potential transmission in North America, where the virus has jumped to cattle, leading to high viral concentrations in milk. Although no confirmed human-to-human transmission has been verified, Krammer warns that a dangerous scenario could arise if a person is co-infected with H5N1 and seasonal influenza, enabling genetic reassortment that could produce a highly transmissible and virulent strain. The 'One Health' approach, which integrates human, animal, and environmental health, is central to addressing the threat. Krammer emphasizes the need for continued monitoring and notes that existing antivirals like Baloxavir and Tamiflu may be effective, and seasonal flu vaccines could be rapidly adapted to target H5N1.

Title: Bird Flu’s Human Risk Spurs Phage Therapy Research

Summary: 
Highly pathogenic avian influenza A (H5N1), commonly known as bird flu, has caused over 633 million bird deaths globally in the past 20 years, with more than 168 million birds lost in the U.S. alone from 2022 to April 2025, according to the USDA's APHIS. The virus has spread to all 50 U.S. states and has spilled over into dairy cows, domestic animals, and marine mammals, affecting over 1,790 dairy herds across 18 states by September 15, 2025, per the Center for Infectious Disease Research and Policy. Human spillovers are rare but documented: 70 cases and one death were reported in the U.S. between March 2024 and May 2025 by the CDC. The CDC warns that due to lack of pre-existing immunity, H5N1 has moderate pandemic potential if it gains efficient human-to-human transmission. In response, researchers are exploring bacteriophage (phage) therapy not only to treat secondary bacterial infections—common in severe flu cases—but also as a platform for developing rapid, scalable vaccines. Cytophage Therapeutics is engineering filamentous phages to display H5N1 epitopes, enabling continuous vaccine production, self-adjuvancy, room-temperature storage, and rapid retooling in days—far faster than mRNA vaccines. PHIOGEN is developing 'dual-action' phages that kill bacteria and stimulate long-term immunity, reducing reinfection risk. Armata is creating fixed multi-phage cocktails using synthetic biology and next-generation sequencing to broaden efficacy and reduce resistance. BiomX uses its AI-driven BOLT platform to screen vast phage libraries and optimize cocktails for potency, host range, and resistance avoidance. The integration of big data, AI, and wet-lab validation enables scalable, precise phage therapies. Experts emphasize that phage therapy's adaptability, safety, and speed make it a uniquely powerful tool for managing secondary infections in avian flu outbreaks and future pandemics.

Title: Review: Human H5N1 avian flu cases can be asymptomatic, and the virus likely spreads among people

Summary: 
A scoping review by researchers from the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), published in JAMA Network Open on October 29, 2025, reveals that asymptomatic human infections with avian influenza A(H5N1) occur and that person-to-person transmission is likely in certain settings. The study analyzed data from 10 reports identifying 18 asymptomatic H5N1 cases, including 2 with molecular and serologic confirmation (MSC) and 16 with molecular confirmation alone (MC). Two MSC cases were identified in adults in Pakistan and Vietnam through household contact investigations; one had exposure to infected poultry, while the other likely contracted the virus through human-to-human transmission, with no poultry contact. Of the 16 MC cases, 11 were found through enhanced surveillance of poultry-exposed individuals (8 in Bangladesh, 2 in Spain, 1 in the UK), and 5 were identified via contact tracing (3 in Vietnam, 2 in Cambodia). The authors emphasize the need for robust data collection from asymptomatic individuals to inform public health responses. In a related commentary, Rick Bright and Nicole Lurie note that since March 2024, H5N1 clade 2.3.4.4b has spread among dairy cattle, with over 800 infected herds in at least 16 US states. As of mid-2025, approximately 70 human cases have been reported, mostly mild, with at least one death. High viral loads have been detected in raw milk, and live virus has been found in mammary tissue and milking equipment. Spillover to other mammals—including cats, dogs, mice, wild carnivores, marine mammals, and swine—has been documented. The authors challenge the traditional view that H5N1 infections in humans are always severe and that human-to-human transmission does not occur, calling attention to a critical gap in surveillance systems that focus on symptomatic illness rather than infection detection, and stressing the importance of investigating clusters for potential limited transmission.

Title: Influenza aviaria in Europa e nel mondo: il monitoraggio di giugno-settembre 2025

Summary: 
The European Food Safety Authority (EFSA) has published a scientific report on highly pathogenic avian influenza (HPAI) in Europe and globally, covering the period from June 7 to September 5, 2025. The report, produced in collaboration with the European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control (ECDC) and the EU Reference Laboratory for Avian Influenza, provides a comprehensive overview of HPAI A(H5) detections in poultry, captive birds, and wild birds across 15 European countries. A total of 183 detections were reported, with the majority (156) occurring in wild birds—particularly in colonial seabirds, especially the European herring gull. There was a noted decline in detections among waterfowl compared to previous months. In poultry, the number of affected farms was lower than in the prior monitoring period (March–June 2025), and no secondary spread of outbreaks was observed. In mammals, four Arctic foxes in Norway tested positive for HPAI A(H5N5). In the United States, HPAI A(H5N1) detections in dairy cattle remained stable, while the muskrat and the round-tailed ground squirrel were reported as newly infected species. Regarding human health, 19 human cases were reported between June 7 and September 5, 2025, including three fatalities, in Bangladesh (1 case of A(H5N1)), Cambodia (11 cases of A(H5N1)), China (1 case of A(H10N3) and 5 cases of A(H9N2)), and India (1 case of A(H5N1)). In most A(H5N1) human cases, exposure to poultry preceded illness. No human-to-human transmission was documented during this period. The risk of infection remains low for the general population in the EU/EEA and low to moderate for individuals with occupational or other exposure to infected animals or contaminated environments. The report concludes that HPAI continues to circulate persistently in wild birds across Europe, with emerging mammalian infections, necessitating sustained surveillance and preventive measures. EFSA recommends long-term risk reduction strategies in poultry farming, such as avoiding high-risk areas for farms, reducing flock density in vulnerable zones, and maintaining high biosecurity standards. EFSA has also launched a new online toolkit: https://www.efsa.europa.eu/en/no-bird-flu.

The CDC’s official avian flu website displayed a notice stating it was 'under revision in accordance with a presidential executive order,' and the agency ceased publishing its vital biweekly H5N1 situation summaries starting January 17, 2025. Although emergency plans claimed essential services would continue, in practice, data collection, analysis, and oversight were halted. The CDC acknowledged delays in monitoring report analysis and inability to guide state and local health departments. Systemic damage included the dismissal of public health inspectors, freezing of NIH research funding reviews, and massive cuts to USAID personnel, leading to the abrupt termination of U.S. surveillance programs in 49 countries. The shutdown, a political choice rather than a natural disaster, turned the public health system into a casualty of partisan conflict, severely undermining the CDC’s credibility as the nation’s source of truth. This erosion of trust—critical during any pandemic—inflicted lasting damage on America’s most vital intangible asset: public confidence in science and government.

articles.title: Review: Human H5N1 avian flu cases can be asymptomatic, and the virus likely spreads among people
articles.summary: A scoping review by researchers from the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), published in JAMA Network Open on October 29, 2025, reveals that asymptomatic human infections with avian influenza A(H5N1) occur and that person-to-person transmission is likely in certain settings. The study analyzed data from 10 reports identifying 18 asymptomatic H5N1 cases, including 2 with molecular and serologic confirmation (MSC) and 16 with molecular confirmation alone (MC). Two MSC cases were identified in adults in Pakistan and Vietnam through household contact investigations; one had exposure to infected poultry, while the other likely contracted the virus through human-to-human transmission, with no poultry contact. Of the 16 MC cases, 11 were found through enhanced surveillance of poultry-exposed individuals (8 in Bangladesh, 2 in Spain, 1 in the UK), and 5 were identified via contact tracing (3 in Vietnam, 2 in Cambodia). The authors emphasize the need for robust data collection from asymptomatic individuals to inform public health responses. In a related commentary, Rick Bright and Nicole Lurie note that since March 2024, H5N1 clade 2.3.4.4b has spread among dairy cattle, with over 800 infected herds in at least 16 US states. As of mid-2025, approximately 70 human cases have been reported, mostly mild, with at least one death. High viral loads have been detected in raw milk, and live virus has been found in mammary tissue and milking equipment. Spillover to other mammals—including cats, dogs, mice, wild carnivores, marine mammals, and swine—has been documented. The authors challenge the traditional view that H5N1 infections in humans are always severe and that human-to-human transmission does not occur, calling attention to a critical gap in surveillance systems that focus on symptomatic illness rather than infection detection, and stressing the importance of investigating clusters for potential limited transmission.

articles.title: Two Mutations Identified That Made Avian Influenza Virus More Dangerous in North America
articles.summary: On March 2024, the first outbreak of highly pathogenic H5N1 avian influenza was detected in dairy cattle in the United States, marking the first time the virus had infected bovine herds. The U.S. Department of Agriculture reports 1,080 cattle cases across 18 states as of September 2025. Human infections have also been documented: 70 cases, primarily among farm workers, with one fatality. A study published in Science Advances identifies two mutations—PB2-478I and NP-450N—in the North American H5N1 clade 2.3.4.4b that increase replication and virulence. Researchers led by Young‑Il Kim at the Korean Center for Emerging Virus Studies performed ferret experiments that showed removal of these mutations prevented systemic infection. The same team demonstrated that viruses carrying the mutations replicated efficiently in human cells and bovine mammary gland cells, underscoring the risk of cross‑species transmission. The authors note, 'Nuestros hallazgos subrayan la necesidad urgente de una vigilancia activa, una preparación e intervenciones dirigidas a mitigar las amenazas zoonóticas y pandémicas.' Aitor Nogales González of CISA, INIA‑CSIC, added, 'Este estudio cuidadosamente diseñado aporta evidencia científica crucial sobre los determinantes genéticos asociados a la virulencia del subtipo H5N1 del virus de la gripe aviar.' The Spanish Society of Emergency Medicine (SEMES) warned of increasing H5N1 outbreaks worldwide, while Spain lost its 'bird‑free' status in July 2025 after outbreaks in several regions. Experts emphasize that, although the risk to the general population remains low, emergency services must be prepared for potential human cases. 'El virus tendría que cambiar bastante, y eso por ahora no ha ocurrido,' explained Inmaculada Casas, noting that the virus is still an animal disease with significant ecological impact.

articles.title: Avian Influenza in Europe and the World: June–September 2025 Monitoring Report
articles.summary: The European Food Safety Authority (EFSA) has published a scientific report on highly pathogenic avian influenza (HPAI) in Europe and globally, covering the period from June 7 to September 5, 2025. The report, produced in collaboration with the European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control (ECDC) and the EU Reference Laboratory for Avian Influenza, provides a comprehensive overview of HPAI A(H5) detections in poultry, captive birds, and wild birds across 15 European countries. A total of 183 detections were reported, with the majority (156) occurring in wild birds—particularly in colonial seabirds, especially the European herring gull. There was a noted decline in detections among waterfowl compared to previous months. In poultry, the number of affected farms was lower than in the prior monitoring period (March–June 2025), and no secondary spread of outbreaks was observed. In mammals, four Arctic foxes in Norway tested positive for HPAI A(H5N5). In the United States, HPAI A(H5N1) detections in dairy cattle remained stable, while the muskrat and the round-tailed ground squirrel were reported as newly infected species. Regarding human health, 19 human cases were reported between June 7 and September 5, 2025, including three fatalities, in Bangladesh (1 case of A(H5N1)), Cambodia (11 cases of A(H5N1)), China (1 case of A(H10N3) and 5 cases of A(H9N2)), and India (1 case of A(H5N1)). In most A(H5N1) human cases, exposure to poultry preceded illness. No human-to-human transmission was documented during this period. The risk of infection remains low for the general population in the EU/EEA and low to moderate for individuals with occupational or other exposure to infected animals or contaminated environments. The report concludes that HPAI continues to circulate persistently in wild birds across Europe, with emerging mammalian infections, necessitating sustained surveillance and preventive measures. EFSA recommends long-term risk reduction strategies in poultry farming, such as avoiding high-risk areas for farms, reducing flock density in vulnerable zones, and maintaining high biosecurity standards. EFSA has also launched a new online toolkit: https://www.efsa.europa.eu/en/no-bird-flu.
